analysis.one_liner: Restores offshore oil and gas leasing in waters President Biden withdrew from drilling.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the Senate Energy Committee without a hearing, vote, or co-sponsor since it was introduced in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: In his final days in office, President Biden issued memoranda permanently withdrawing large areas of the outer Continental Shelf—the Gulf of Mexico, the Atlantic and Pacific coasts, and parts of the Bering Sea—from new oil and gas leasing. This bill would wipe those memoranda out, making it legal again for the federal government to sell offshore drilling leases in those waters. It was introduced by Sen. Ted Cruz with no co-sponsors and referred to the Senate Energy Committee, where nothing has happened since.
analysis.who_benefits: Offshore oil and gas companies would gain access to lease new federal waters for exploration and drilling in the Gulf of Mexico, along the Atlantic and Pacific coasts, and in the Bering Sea — territory worth billions in future production. Some supporters argue broader domestic drilling could modestly lower energy prices over the long run, though new offshore leases take years to produce.

how_it_helps.text: It would re-open hundreds of millions of offshore acres—Gulf of Mexico, Atlantic, Pacific, and Bering Sea—to oil and gas leasing by nullifying the January 6, 2025 withdrawals.
It would restore the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management's authority to issue offshore leases for exploration, development, and production in those areas.

analysis.who_pays: Coastal communities and the public would bear the risks of expanded offshore drilling — oil spill exposure for fisheries, beaches, and tourism — while the leasing revenue and production profits flow to the industry. Any environmental damage from drilling in newly opened waters would be effectively permanent.

drawbacks.text: Rescinding the withdrawal would open vast areas of the Gulf of Mexico, Atlantic, Pacific, and Bering Sea to offshore drilling, with the spill and environmental risks those waters carry falling on coastal communities and fisheries rather than on the leasing companies.

The bill is drafted as a nullification of presidential memoranda rather than a leasing plan, so it would not by itself guarantee any new leases or lower energy prices; it simply removes the legal barrier to offering them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside would be more domestic oil production and possibly lower energy-industry costs; the downside is locking in decades more offshore drilling in waters where a spill would damage coasts and fishing economies that cannot be made whole afterward. Because the ban's rescission is a one-way door—leased areas are hard to re-protect—the asymmetry of risk falls on the public while the reward accrues to a narrow set of producers. The bill has no co-sponsors and no committee action, so it has not advanced far enough for these tradeoffs to be tested in debate.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on January 15, 2025 and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, where it has stayed ever since—no hearing, no vote, and not a single co-signer.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 15, 2025, read twice, and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
No further action has been taken: the action history shows nothing after the referral, so the committee has never voted on it and it has never reached the Senate floor.
No senator has signed on as a co-sponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies wanting to drill in the withdrawn federal waters are no worse off, since the bill went nowhere; the protections in the Biden memoranda remain in place for now, though the underlying question of offshore leasing remains politically live.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coastal protections held; drillers gained nothing

for.name: Sen. Ted Cruz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to nullify the offshore leasing withdrawals.

sides.party_line_note: Only the sponsor's action is in the record; no co-sponsors, no committee action, and no votes, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.note: Rescinding the withdrawal re-opens federal waters to leasing, the main channel through which offshore drillers acquire acreage. Nothing in the bill regulates them further; it purely removes a restriction on where they can bid. Its interest runs against the coastal and environmental protections ordinary people get from the ban.
Opening these waters to drilling exposes beaches and fisheries to spill risk and industrial activity, with no offsetting benefit written into the bill for the communities bearing that risk.

industries.industry: Offshore wind and clean energy development
industries.note: The memoranda withdrawn by this bill relate only to oil and gas leasing, so the direct effect on wind is limited, but renewed drilling activity in shared waters can compete for ocean space, ports, and regulatory attention.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has no co-sponsors and no committee activity since referral. Bills at this stage with a single sponsor and no hearing rarely advance; it is likely to remain stalled unless offshore leasing becomes a priority for committee leadership. The administration could also reverse the memoranda on its own, making the bill moot.
